MOBY-DICK; OR, THE WHALE
Herman Melville

CHAPTER 1. LOOMINGS

Call me Ishmael. Some years ago—never mind how long precisely—having little or no money in my
purse, and nothing particular to interest me on shore, I thought I would sail about a little
and see the watery part of the world. It is a way I have of driving off the spleen and
regulating the circulation. Whenever I find myself growing grim about the mouth; whenever it
is a damp, drizzly November in my soul; whenever I find myself involuntarily pausing before
coffin warehouses and bringing up the rear of every funeral I meet; and especially whenever my
temper requires a strong moral principle to prevent me from deliberately stepping into the
street and knocking people's hats off—then, I account it high time to get to sea as soon as I
can.

There is magic in water. Take almost any path you please, and ten to one it carries you down in
a dale and leaves you by a pool in the stream. Stand a man on his legs, set his feet going, and
he will infallibly lead you to water if water there be in all that region. Meditation and water
are wedded forever.

I was not drawn to sea as a passenger. To go as a passenger one must have a purse, and a purse
is but a rag unless one has something in it. Besides, passengers get sea-sick, grow quarrelsome,
sleep of nights, and do not enjoy themselves much. Nor would I go as a commodore, captain, or
cook. I abandon the glory and distinction of such offices to those who like them. No, when I go
to sea, I go as a simple sailor, right before the mast, plumb down into the forecastle, aloft
there to the royal mast-head.

CHAPTER 2. THE CARPET-BAG

I stuffed a shirt or two into my old carpet-bag, tucked it under my arm, and started for Cape
Horn and the Pacific. Quitting the good city of old Manhatto, I duly arrived in New Bedford. It
was a Saturday night in December. Much was I disappointed upon learning that the little packet
for Nantucket had already sailed and that no way of reaching that place would offer until the
following Monday.

Now, lodging for the night was the next question. It looked very dubious and dark. With anxious
grapnels I had sounded my pocket and brought up only a few pieces of silver. I wandered about
the streets, pausing before the bright windows of expensive inns and returning to the blackness
outside. At last I came to a dim sign bearing a white, swinging painting of a tall straight jet
of misty spray and the words, The Spouter-Inn.

CHAPTER 3. THE SPOUTER-INN

Entering that gable-ended place, I found a wide, low, straggling entry with old-fashioned
wainscots reminding one of the bulwarks of some condemned ship. On one side hung a very large
oil-painting so thoroughly besmoked and defaced that only by diligent study could any meaning
be made of it. A long, limber, portentous black mass hovered in the centre of three blue,
dimly-perceived lines floating in a nameless yeast. What the painting meant no one could tell
at once; but by degrees a final theory came: a ship foundering in a great hurricane, with an
enormous whale impaling itself upon the masts.

The landlord told me there was no private room. I might share the bed of a harpooneer. The idea
was alarming enough, but the cold streets were worse. I waited while the hours lengthened and
the stranger did not return. When at last I climbed into the bed alone, I hoped to be asleep
before my unknown companion arrived.

He came after midnight carrying a strange wooden idol and a heavy bag. In the uncertain light
his tattooed face and unfamiliar customs startled me into a cry. The harpooneer was no less
startled to find another man in his bed. The landlord burst in laughing, introduced him as
Queequeg, and assured us we would become good friends. Exhaustion settled the matter. By
morning, Queequeg's arm lay over me in a friendly and protective manner, and the terrors of the
night looked very different in daylight.
